paragraphs.text: A cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yunnan, made in 2007 from sun-dried maocha and listed in the shop as humid-stored, the practice the trade calls [shi cang, or humid storage](sheng:storage). Raw pu’er changes partly through slow oxidation and partly through the work of microbes. Warmth and moisture speed both, so a humid store reaches in fewer years what a dry, cool one takes far longer to reach. In the twentieth century, merchants in Hong Kong, then pu’er’s great drinking market, kept their tea this way [to hasten its change](sheng:history). The trade still does not agree whether humid storage is a flaw or a style of its own.

At nineteen years, this cake sits where the trade begins to argue about [aged raw pu’er](sheng:ageing). Some count from ten years, while many wait for twenty or more. Because raw pu’er is never put through shou’s rapid fermentation, its [storage belongs to its history](sheng:aging). A humid store is not a promise of quality.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
